# Results — Study 650 (Heating-Oil-Seasonality)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **heating
oil rallies into winter** on cold-weather distillate demand, in two named stages: an **autumn
build** (Sep-Nov, the market pricing the coming season ahead of time) and a **winter draw**
(Dec-Feb, physical inventories fall as furnaces run). Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete
calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprints `5e77c79ac501` (HO=F)
/ `f140d3086a31` (UHN) / `97d049b701d7` (^IRX).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily HO=F raw OHLC (6,484 rows), 2000-09-01 → 2026-06-30 — Yahoo's continuous front-month chain, **not** back-adjusted (the roll splice is the term-structure cost/gain a real futures roller pays, by construction); UHN adjusted closes (2,625 rows), 2008-04-10 → 2018-09-11 (its full trading life — USCF wound the fund down; not extended); ^IRX closes (6,487 rows), 2000-09-01 → 2026-06-30 |
| Calendar | **hardcoded** heating-season windows — autumn-build = Sep–Nov, winter-draw = Dec–Feb, heating window = Sep–Feb (their union), off-season = Mar–Aug. A calendar fact, not a fitted parameter |
| Sample | HO=F monthly returns, month-end daily-close resample, **309 months** 2000-10 → 2026-06, hole-free grid |
| Statistics | one-sample *t* per calendar month (Bonferroni-12 bar |*t*| ≥ ~3.0, α=0.05/12 two-sided at n≈25); Welch *t* for the three group splits (autumn-build / winter-draw / heating window vs off-season) |
| Execution / costs | seasonal timer: enter the heating window at Sep 1 (the calendar needs no lookahead — it is a fixed rule, not a forecast), exit end-Feb, T-bill (^IRX/12) otherwise; one-way cost × NAV charged at each of the 2 switches/yr |
| Data quirks (named) | HO=F is a **spliced continuous chain** — no back-adjustment — so the daily return on a roll day already contains the contango/backwardation cost a real futures holder would pay; UHN's trading life **ends 2018-09-11** (product wound down, not extended, not survivorship-adjusted) |

No survivorship on the Signal axis: HO=F is a futures chain, not a basket of survivors.
**Named on the third axis:** UHN is the *actual retail vehicle* for this trade and it no longer
exists — any UHN-based backtest necessarily stops in 2018, and a reader today literally cannot
buy the fund that would have expressed this claim.

## The headline — per-calendar-month mean HO=F return (one-sample *t* vs 0)

| month | mean | *t* | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Jan | +2.49% | +1.25 | 26 |
| Feb | +3.26% | +1.39 | 26 |
| Mar | +1.22% | +0.36 | 26 |
| Apr | +1.65% | +0.77 | 26 |
| May | −0.26% | −0.12 | 26 |
| **Jun** | **+3.14%** | **+2.33** | 26 |
| Jul | +1.08% | +0.64 | 25 |
| Aug | +2.23% | +1.49 | 25 |
| Sep | +0.13% | +0.07 | 25 |
| Oct | −0.78% | −0.40 | 26 |
| Nov | −2.12% | −1.02 | 26 |
| Dec | −0.41% | −0.21 | 26 |

**No month clears the Bonferroni-12 bar** (|*t*| ≥ ~3.0). The only month that clears the naive
|*t*| ≥ 2 house bar is **June** (*t* = +2.33) — the middle of driving season, not a heating
month, and it still fails Bonferroni. Every heating-season month (Sep–Feb) sits at |*t*| < 1.5.

## Group tests — autumn-build / winter-draw / heating window vs off-season (Welch *t*)

| window | mean | n | vs off-season (Mar–Aug, +1.51%, n=154) | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|---|--:|
| autumn-build (Sep–Nov) | **−0.94%** | 77 | wrong sign | **−1.71** |
| winter-draw (Dec–Feb) | +1.78% | 78 | right sign, not significant | +0.18 |
| heating window (Sep–Feb) | +0.43% | 155 | wrong sign (under-performs off-season) | −0.89 |

The two halves of the claim don't even agree with each other: the "autumn build" is actually
the **worst** three-month stretch on the calendar (−0.94%, wrong sign, *t* = −1.71 — closer to
significant than any other test in this study, and pointing the *wrong* way), while the
"winter draw" is unremarkable (+0.18). Pooled, the heating window **under-performs** the
off-season it's supposed to beat. No test clears |*t*| ≥ 2 in the claimed direction.

## Tradability — seasonal timer (long Sep–Feb, T-bill otherwise) vs buy-and-hold

Sharpe = excess of the rolled 13-week T-bill, both legs; costs = one-way bps × NAV per switch
(2 switches/yr — enter Sep, exit end-Feb).

| strategy | CAGR | Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| buy & hold HO=F | **+5.06%** | **0.27** | −81% |
| seasonal timer, gross | +0.29% | 0.07 | −72% |
| seasonal timer, net 5 bps | +0.19% | 0.06 | −72% |
| seasonal timer, net 10 bps | +0.08% | 0.06 | −73% |

The timer isn't just beaten by costs — it's beaten by the null hypothesis. **Even gross, before
a single basis point of cost**, sitting in cash for six months a year (Mar–Aug, precisely the
months HO=F actually earns its keep — June alone averages +3.1%) throws away roughly four-fifths
of buy-and-hold's Sharpe. Costs are almost irrelevant here: the strategy is broken by
construction, not by friction.

## Third axis — the real retail vehicle (UHN) vs the HO=F splice, paired per heating season

UHN (United States Heating Oil Fund, USCF) held front-month HO=F futures directly for retail,
2008-04-10 → 2018-09-11 (its whole life; **the fund no longer exists**). Paired per season
(Aug 31 close → next Feb 28 close), `gap = UHN return − HO=F splice return` over the identical
calendar dates:

| season | UHN | HO=F splice | gap |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 2008–2009 | −60.72% | −58.81% | −1.90% |
| 2009–2010 | +4.31% | +13.81% | −9.50% |
| 2010–2011 | +42.58% | +46.70% | −4.12% |
| 2011–2012 | +4.35% | +4.73% | −0.38% |
| 2012–2013 | −6.66% | −6.24% | −0.42% |
| 2013–2014 | −0.35% | −1.87% | +1.52% |
| 2014–2015 | −23.18% | −17.80% | −5.38% |
| 2015–2016 | −43.38% | −37.19% | −6.19% |
| 2016–2017 | +7.57% | +14.93% | −7.36% |
| 2017–2018 | +10.79% | +8.88% | +1.91% |
| **mean / *t*** | | | **−3.18%/season, *t* = −2.58 (n=10, small sample)** |

The wrapper lost money relative to the futures splice in **8 of 10** heating seasons — the
expense ratio and tracking slippage stack a second, real drag *on top of* the roll cost already
embedded in HO=F. The one-sample *t* (−2.58 on n=10) is not certifiable at this sample size —
said out loud — but the direction is consistent and the sign of the point estimate never helps
the claim.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic i.i.d. monthly-return world with a TUNABLE planted heating-season premium spread
over Sep–Feb; no network.

| world | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|
| null (seasonal = 0), **20 seeds** (base 1000) | mean **−0.19** (sd 1.01), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 0/20 seeds** |
| planted seasonal = +0.15 (seed 650) | **+3.61** |

The detector never fires on the null and lights up cleanly on a planted premium comparable in
size to a real seasonal claim. *(A faithful-engine / power check only — never cited in support
of a real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** No calendar month clears the Bonferroni-12 bar; the naive |*t*| ≥ 2 bar is
  cleared only by June (not a heating month). The autumn-build window is **negative and the
  wrong sign** (−0.94%, *t* = −1.71 — the single closest-to-significant number in the whole
  study, pointing *against* the folklore); the winter-draw window is unremarkable (*t* = +0.18);
  pooled, the heating window under-performs the off-season it's supposed to beat (*t* = −0.89).
  Twenty-six years of HO=F data give no statistically real, correctly-signed month-of-year
  seasonal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A seasonal timer built exactly as the folklore prescribes (long
  Sep–Feb, cash otherwise) loses roughly four-fifths of buy-and-hold's Sharpe **before any
  cost is charged** (0.07 vs 0.27), and the one real retail vehicle that ever existed for this
  trade (UHN) lost money against the futures splice in 8 of its 10 seasons before it was wound
  down in 2018 — it is not buyable today at any price.
- **"Heating oil rallies into winter" — the trader's rule of thumb? — BUSTED.** Not weak, not
  regime-dependent — the autumn half of the claim runs backward on the tape, the winter half is
  noise, and the one product built to sell it to retail no longer exists.
